summary: Defines a MIB module of textual conventions for commonly used GMPLS management information. Other GMPLS MIB modules can import them instead of defining their own.

eli5.summary: When many forms need the same kind of box, you design the box once. This defines shared building blocks used by other GMPLS management lists.

questions: what is a textual convention in a mib
subtitle: Shared MIB building blocks for describing labels and LSP direction in GMPLS management modules.

tldr.problem: Several GMPLS-related MIB modules need to represent the same things, such as labels and the direction of data on a path, and would otherwise each define their own versions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4801 defines the GMPLS-TC-STD-MIB module with three textual conventions: GmplsFreeformLabelTC, GmplsLabelTypeTC and GmplsSegmentDirectionTC, which other modules import.
tldr.outcome: The module defines no managed objects of its own, so it only provides shared definitions, and it supplements the MPLS textual conventions of RFC 3811.

today: RFC 4801 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose of the Module
sections.content:
RFC 4801 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module of textual conventions (TCs) for Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) networks. MIB modules that manage GMPLS networks should import them rather than define their own representations.

It supplements the MIB module in RFC 3811, which defines textual conventions for MPLS management. RFC 3811 may continue to be used without this module in networks that support only MPLS. For an introduction to GMPLS concepts, the RFC points to RFC 3945.
sections.eli5: It makes a set of shared definitions so every GMPLS management list describes the same things in the same way.

sections.title: The Management Framework
sections.content: Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store called the Management Information Base. MIB objects are generally accessed using the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), and are defined using the Structure of Management Information (SMI). This module is compliant with SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. For the wider framework the RFC refers to section 7 of RFC 3410.
sections.eli5: Network gear keeps a big list of things you can look at and change. SMI is the rulebook for how entries in that list are written down.

sections.title: The Three Labels-and-Direction Conventions
sections.content:
The module is named gmplsTCStdMIB and sits under mplsStdMIB. It imports MODULE-IDENTITY from SNMPv2-SMI, TEXTUAL-CONVENTION from SNMPv2-TC and mplsStdMIB from MPLS-TC-STD-MIB. It defines three conventions.

  • GmplsFreeformLabelTC: an OCTET STRING (SIZE (0..64)) that can hold any GMPLS label. It can represent labels of types not defined in any RFC, and systems may use it instead of type-specific syntaxes.
  • GmplsLabelTypeTC: an integer saying how to interpret an object that encodes a label.
  • GmplsSegmentDirectionTC: the direction of data flow on a Label Switched Path (LSP) segment relative to the head of the LSP, either forward(1) or reverse(2).
sections.eli5: There are three shared pieces: a box that can hold any label, a note saying what kind of label is in it, and an arrow showing which way the traffic goes.

sections.title: Label Types and Segment Direction
sections.content:
GmplsLabelTypeTC has six values:

  • gmplsMplsLabel(1): an MPLS packet, cell or frame label, encoded as the MplsLabel convention in RFC 3811.
  • gmplsPortWavelengthLabel(2): a port or wavelength label as defined in RFC 3471.
  • Value 3: a label of any form encoded as an octet string using the freeform convention.
  • gmplsSonetLabel(4) and gmplsSdhLabel(5): SONET and SDH labels as defined in RFC 4606.
  • gmplsWavebandLabel(6): a waveband label as defined in RFC 3471.

For GmplsSegmentDirectionTC, the head of an LSP signaled with a conventional protocol is the source of the signaling (the ingress) and the tail is the destination (the egress). For unidirectional LSPs this usually matches the data direction. For manually configured bidirectional LSPs, an arbitrary decision must be made about which LER is the head. Forward means data flows from head toward tail, reverse the opposite.

The description text names value 3 gmplsFreeformLabel(3) while the SYNTAX clause lists gmplsFreeformGeneralizedLabel(3). Both use the number 3.
sections.eli5: The label-type note is a sticker on the box: MPLS, wavelength, SONET and so on. The direction arrow says whether traffic runs from the start of the path to the end, or back.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The module defines no management objects, only textual conventions that other GMPLS MIB modules use. The RFC says meaningful security considerations can only be written in the modules that define the objects, so this document has no impact on the security of the Internet.

IANA assigned the OID for gmplsTCStdMIB as number 12 under mplsStdMIB (1.3.6.1.2.1.10.166). Future GMPLS-related standards-track MIB modules should be rooted under the same subtree, and new assignments need a Standards Action.
sections.eli5: This module is only a set of definitions, so it cannot be attacked directly. Safety rules belong in the lists that actually use it.
